new_statements.rule_in_words: Second-hand typological filing only: main stress on the word-initial syllable; the compiler had no information on secondary stress. Deduced by Goedemans from Austin's 1992 Warriyangga dictionary (not seen by me). The closest first-hand statement, for sister-language Jiwarli (UniMelb/Austin 2001 web site), is initial stress except that a long vowel in a non-initial syllable takes the stress; Austin 2015 notes long vowels in Mantharta are 'typically found in the first syllable'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Goedemans: 'no info on sec stress' for Warriyanka.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Warriyangka. (For Jiwarli, the UniMelb site says stress falls on whichever syllable contains a long vowel.)
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level typological classification; no phonetic or phrase-level detail. Underlying data for Warriyangka are very limited (O'Grady 1958/1967 recordings; one semi-speaker recorded by Austin 1978).
new_statements.identity_note: Spellings: Warriyangka (Austin 1988-2015), Warriyangga (Austin 1992 dictionary title; Glottolog 'Wariyangga'), Warriyanka (Goedemans 1998), Wariengga/Warianga (O'Grady); Tindale T66, AIATSIS W22. Austin 1988 treats Malykaru as a dialect. Documentation is thin: O'Grady 1958/1967 recordings and one semi-speaker (Stuart Peck) recorded by Austin in 1978. The only first-hand stress statement located in the Mantharta group is for the sister language Jiwarli (djiw1241; c. 80% shared vocabulary per Austin 2006), not for wari1262: UniMelb/Austin Jiwarli web site (2001): 'Whereas the stress in Jiwarli is nearly always on the first syllable, the stress in words with long vowels is on whichever syllable contains the long vowel.' Austin's 2015 Mantharta grammar treats Jiwarli, Thiin and Warriyangka as 'structurally similar' in phonology (vs. divergent Tharrkari) but says nothing about stress.
